question_text: A 58-year-old male presented with weakness of the lower half of the right side of the face with drooping of angle of mouth. He is able to raise his eyebrows and close eyes on both sides. Which of the following is the likely site of the lesion?
option_a: Infranuclear facial nerve palsy on right side
option_b: Supranuclear facial nerve palsy on right side
option_c: Infranuclear facial nerve palsy on left side
option_d: Supranuclear facial nerve palsy on left side
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient is able to raise his eyebrows and close his eyes on both sides but has weakness in left lower half of face which is suggestive of supranuclear facial nerve palsy on the left side.

  • The nucleus supplying the upper face muscles receives bilateral cortical innervation. Due to this,in supranuclear facial nerve palsy the upper face muscles on the affected side will be spared because they still receive innervation from the unaffected cerebral hemisphere.
  • The nucleus supplying the lower face muscles receives contralateral cortical innervation only. Consequently, a lesion in one cerebral hemisphere will result in weakness of the lower half of the face on the contralateral side.

Since this patient's symptoms are on the right side, the lesion is likely on the left side.

Explanation of Other Options:

Infranuclear facial nerve palsy on the right side (Option A)

An infranuclear lesion on the right would cause weakness of the entire right face (both upper and lower). This does not match the patient's spared right upper face.

Supranuclear facial nerve palsy on right side (Option B)

Supranuclear facial palsy on the right side typically causes weakness of only the lower half of the face on the left side, sparing the forehead (because of bilateral cortical innervation). This patient has symptoms on the right side.

Infranuclear facial nerve palsy on left side (Option C)

Infranuclear facial nerve palsy on the left side would cause weakness of entire left face (both upper and lower). This does not match the patient's symptoms, which are on the right side.

Key Takeaway:

A supranuclear lesion on the left side of the brain typically causes contralateral weakness predominantly affecting the lower half of the right face. The right upper face is spared due to bilateral cortical innervation.

The cranial outflow of the autonomic nervous system refers to parasympathetic nervous fibers, which do not control the tone of the vasculature. Dorsal roots of cervical nerves carry afferent sensory fibers, not sympathetic neurons. The grey rami communicantes are structures that postganglionic sympathetic neurons travel on before rejoining a spinal nerve, so destroying the grey rami communicantes might disrupt the sympathetic outflow. This could be a good answer, except that the T5 spinal nerve will have no effect on the side of the face. question_text: Which muscle is innervated by posterior primary rami?
explanation:
Of all the answer choices, erector spinae is the only true back muscle listed. True back muscles act on the vertebral column, producing its movements and maintaining posture. These true back muscles are innervated by posterior (dorsal) primary rami. The other four muscles are superficial back muscles that aid with the movements of the limbs as well as with respiration. They mostly receive their nerve supply from the ventral rami of cervical nerves. Latissimus dorsi is innervated by the thoracodorsal nerve, which is made from branches of the ventral primary rami of C5 and C6. Levator scapulae and rhomboideus major are innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve, a branch of the ventral primary rami of C5. (The superior part of levator scapulae also receives some innervation from the ventral primary rami of C3 and C4.) Lastly, trapezius is innervated by the accessory nerve (CN XI) but also receives innervation from C3 and C4 ventral primary rami for proprioception.

question_text: A 40 year-old woman has difficulty swallowing and frequently aspirates fluids while drinking. She is diagnosed as having a skull base tumor occupying the space behind the jugular foramen. Involvement of which structure is responsible for the findings?
explanation:
The vagus nerve, which exits the skull through the jugular foramen, is the motor nerve to the pharynx. So, it allows for swallowing. This patient's symptoms and the location of the tumor clearly point to an injury of the vagus nerve. The accessory nerve also exits the skull through the jugular foramen, it could be injured from this tumor, but the symptoms are not suggestive of an accessory nerve injury. If her accessory nerve was damaged, the patient's sternocleidomastoid and trapezius would be denervated, which means the acromion of her shoulder would sag. The other nerve that comes through the jugular foramen is the glossopharyngeal nerve, this nerve might also be damaged by the tumor.

Explanation:

The spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) supplies the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles. Difficulty in shoulder shrugging and head rotation, as seen in this patient, indicates injury to this nerve. Trauma from the nail could have damaged or compressed the spinal accessory nerve, resulting in the observed symptoms.

Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) details:

  • Supplies: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles
  • Pathway: Enters cranial cavity via foramen magnum and exits via jugular foramen
  • Anatomical relevance: Passes through the occipital triangle
  • Clinical sign of injury: Weakness in shoulder shrugging due to trapezius involvement

Explanation of other options:

Deltoid Muscle (Option B): Responsible primarily for shoulder abduction. Dysfunction of the deltoid does not cause difficulty in shrugging the shoulders or turning the head, so it is not consistent with this scenario.

Sternocleidomastoid Muscle (Option C): Involved in rotation and flexion of the head. While it contributes to neck movement, it does not control shoulder shrugging. An isolated SCM injury would not explain both observed symptoms.

Long Thoracic Nerve (Option D): Innervates the serratus anterior muscle. Damage results in scapular winging (protrusion of the scapula), which is not seen in this patient.

question_text: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a fractured mandible after a bar fight. After the mandibular reconstruction surgery, the patient is noted to have loss of sensation in his lower lip. After further testing, it is determined that the patient has damage to the mandibular branch of his trigeminal nerve. Which of the following symptoms would also likely fit this diagnosis?
option_a: Loss of sensation of the upper lip
option_c: Ability to forcefully close the eyes is diminished
option_d: Loss of sensation in the tip of the tongue
explanation:
Along with providing sensation to the lower lip, the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve also provides sensation to the mandibular gums and teeth, as well as the anterior surface of the tongue via the lingual nerve branch. Thus, damage to V3 would cause loss of sensation in the tip of the tongue.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and neck, page number - 985

question_text: A 42-year-old female who had the extraction of her 3rd molar tooth reported loss of sensation in the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue and floor of the mouth. Which nerve is most likely to be damaged?
explanation:
Explanation: 

The lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), supplies general sensory innervation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and the floor of the mouth. Injury to this nerve is a recognized complication during the extraction of the third molar, leading to numbness or loss of sensation in these areas.

Explanation of other options:

Glossopharyngeal Nerve (Option B): Supplies taste and general sensation to the posterior one-third of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds or floor of the mouth.

Spinal Accessory Nerve (Option C): Controls sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles; unrelated to tongue or mouth floor sensation.

Chorda Tympani Nerve (Option D): A Branch of the facial nerve (VII) that carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers to salivary glands. It does not provide sensation to the floor of the mouth and is rarely injured during dental procedures.

question_text: While doing a postoperative physical on a patient who has undergone carotid endarterectomy on the right side, it was noted that the tongue deviated toward the right when the patient was asked to point the tongue outward. What nerve crossing the carotid artery must have been injured?
explanation:
The hypoglossal nerve crosses the carotid artery before diving into the floor of the mouth, so it might get injured during this procedure. This nerve innervates the muscles of the tongue. When the hypoglossal nerve is injured and a patient sticks out the tongue, the tongue points to the side with the injured nerve. So, this patient, who had the right side endarctectomy, has an injury to the right hypoglossal nerve. The symptoms that you see in this case should point you toward suspecting damage to the hypoglossal nerve.

The glossopharyngeal nerve crosses around the internal carotid artery and the stylopharyngeus muscle, it could theoretically be injured in this procedure, but the symptoms are not consistent with an injury to this structure. The inferior alveolar nerve and lingual nerves are branches of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. They are not associated with the carotid vessels. The vagus nerve is found in the carotid sheath. This nerve can be easily injured by an endarterectomy, although damage to the vagus would cause problems with swallowing, not with tongue movements.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and neck, Page number - 900

question_text: Which of the following cranial nerves form the afferent limb of corneal reflex?
explanation:
The trigeminal nerve forms the afferent limb of the corneal reflex.

  • The corneal reflex is elicited clinically by gentle touching of the cornea with wisp of cotton wool.
  • As the cornea is touched both the eyes are closed.
  • Pathway:
    • Ophthalmic nerve (afferent limb)
    • Main sensory nucleus of trigeminal nerve
    • Reticular formation
    • Both the facial nerves (efferent limbs)
  • The facial nerve stimulates orbicularis oculi muscle resulting in a blink.

Explanation for Other Options:

Trochlear nerve (Option D)

The trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV) is a motor nerve innervating the superior oblique muscle of the eye and is unrelated to the corneal reflex pathway.

Key Takeaways:

The corneal reflex's afferent limb is carried by the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve, which senses corneal stimulation and triggers the reflexive blinking response via the facial nerve as the efferent limb.

question_text: A patient presents with a unilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, and excessive lacrimation. He also complains of hemifacial pain on the clenching of teeth. On examination, pupillary reaction, light reflex, and accommodation reflex are normal. Which of the following marked nerves is involved in the above scenario?
explanation:
Explanation:

The constellation of symptoms-including facial pain triggered by jaw movement and autonomic signs like lacrimation-points to involvement of the ophthalmic division (V₁) of the trigeminal nerve, which innervates the upper face, eye region, and conveys ocular sensory signals

Trigeminal nerve (5th cranial nerve): Has three divisions

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

  • 1(Option A): (Most likely corresponds to V₂ or V₃)-These divisions supply the mid- and lower face or motor areas such as jaw muscles. They do not normally trigger lacrimation or photophobia, nor do they involve pain in the upper face or ocular region.
  • 2 (Option B): (Likely V₂)-This division innervates the middle third of the face-cheeks, upper lip, upper teeth-but doesn't supply the forehead, eye region, or induce lacrimation or light sensitivity.
  • 4 (Option D): (Likely V₃)-The mandibular branch affects lower facial sensation and mastication muscles. While clenching may trigger pain via V₃, the additional signs of headache, photophobia, or autonomic lacrimation point toward V₁ involvement.

question_text: A 12-year-old boy presents with a history of ptosis of the right upper eyelid since birth. On examination, the right eye is deviated downward and outward at rest. Which of the following cranial nerve palsies best explains these findings?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) supplies most of the extraocular muscles (superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique), as well as the levator palpebrae superioris (responsible for eyelid elevation) and carries parasympathetic fibers for pupil constriction.

When the 3rd nerve is paralyzed:

  • The only unopposed muscles are lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV), which pull the eye down and out.
  • Paralysis of levator palpebrae superioris causes ptosis.
  • Thus, the combination of ptosis with a down-and-out eye is characteristic of 3rd nerve palsy.

Explanation of other options:

4th nerve palsy (Option A): Causes defective downward gaze in adduction (superior oblique paralysis), not a down-and-out resting position.

6th nerve palsy (Option C): Leads to inability to abduct the eye (lateral rectus paralysis), but does not cause ptosis.

7th nerve palsy (Option D): Affects muscles of facial expression, not extraocular muscles, so the eye position is normal.

question_text: A woman presented with sudden onset of dysphagia, dysarthria, and gait ataxia. MRI revealed an acute infarct in the right dorsolateral medulla. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

An infarct in the dorsolateral medulla is characteristic of Wallenberg syndrome (Lateral Medullary Syndrome), typically caused by occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral artery.

The presented symptoms align perfectly with this syndrome:

Dysphagia and dysarthria (due to involvement of the nucleus ambiguus affecting CN IX and X) and gait ataxia (due to involvement of the inferior cerebellar peduncle and spinocerebellar tracts).

Other classic findings include ipsilateral Horner's syndrome and loss of facial pain/temperature sensation, with contralateral loss of bodily pain/temperature sensation.

Explanation of other options:

Dejerine's anterior bulbar syndrome (Option A): This is a medial medullary syndrome affecting the pyramidal tract, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nerve, leading to contralateral hemiparesis and ipsilateral tongue palsy, not the symptoms described.

Babinski-Nageotte syndrome (Option C): This involves both medullary and pontine structures, resulting in a complex mix of lateral and medial signs not typical for a pure dorsolateral infarct.

Weber syndrome (Option D): This is a midbrain syndrome involving the cerebral peduncle and oculomotor nerve, causing ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral hemiparesis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Wallenberg syndrome results from a lateral medullary infarct.
  • Key features include dysphagia, dysarthria, ataxia, and crossed sensory deficits.

question_text: Which option correctly pairs a compartment of this foramen with its contents?
explanation:
The jugular foramen may be subdivided into three compartments, each with their own contents.

  • The anterior compartment transmits the inferior petrosal sinus.
  • The intermediate compartment transmits the glossopharyngeal nerve, the vagus nerve, and the accessory nerve.
  • The posterior compartment transmits the sigmoid sinus (becoming the internal jugular vein), and some meningeal branches from the occipital artery and ascending pharyngeal artery.

Explanation of Other Options:

Posterior compartment - Accessory nerve (Option B): The accessory nerve (CN XI) passes through the intermediate compartment along with CN IX and X. The posterior compartment transmits the sigmoid sinus.

Intermediate compartment - Ascending pharyngeal artery (Option C): Meningeal branches of the ascending pharyngeal artery pass through the posterior compartment. The intermediate compartment is reserved for cranial nerves.

Anterior compartment - Vagus nerve (Option D): The vagus nerve (CN X) passes through the intermediate compartment.

The contents of the jugular foramen can be summarized as follows:

Key Takeaways:

  • Anterior compartment: Think veins (inferior petrosal sinus).
  • Intermediate compartment: Think nerves (CN IX, X, XI).
  • Posterior compartment: Think veins and arteries (sigmoid sinus/IJV and small meningeal arteries).

Reference:

Gray's Anatomy for Students: Volume 2, 3rd Edition, Page Number: 864.

question_text: The vagus nerve passes into the abdomen by passing through the
explanation:
Remember back to the thorax--the vagus joins the esophageal plexus and covers the esophagus. The anterior and posterior vagal trunks form from the esophageal plexus-- they pass into the abdomen through the esophageal hiatus, on the anterior and posterior surfaces of the esophagus. The aortic hiatus is deep to the median arcuate ligament--it transmits the aorta and the thoracic duct. Psoas major is deep to the medial arcuate ligament, and quadratus lumborum is deep to the lateral arcuate ligament.

question_text: A 60-year-old male presents with loss of sensation over the marked area shown in the figure. Which nerve is most likely affected?
explanation:
Explanation:

The concha of the external ear is supplied by the auricular branch of the vagus nerve (also called Alderman's nerve). Loss of sensation in this region indicates damage to this nerve.

Sensory Supply of the External Ear (Lateral Surface):

  • Upper two-thirds: Auriculotemporal nerve (branch of CN V3) (Option B)
  • Lower one-third: Greater auricular nerve (C2, C3) (Option A)
  • Concha and eminentia conchae: Auricular branch of vagus nerve (Alderman's nerve)

Motor Supply:

  • Facial nerve supplies the small auricular muscles. (Option D)

The concha region is unique because it is the only part of the external ear supplied by the vagus nerve, which explains the cough reflex sometimes triggered by cleaning this area.

Key Takeaway:

The auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Alderman's nerve) is responsible for sensory innervation to the concha of the ear, making it the affected nerve in this patient with loss of sensation in that area.

question_text: All of the following structures present in interpeduncular fossa, EXCEPT:
explanation:
Explanation:

The interpeduncular fossa contains tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, infundibulum, posterior perforated substance, and the oculomotor nerve (CNIII). The trochlear nerve (CNIV) does not lie here, it emerges dorsally from the midbrain. Hence, option C is the only structure not present in the interpeduncular fossa.

question_text: Which of the following structure is not passing through the superior orbital fissure?
explanation:
Explanation:

The superior orbital fissure is the gap between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid, bounded medially by the body of the sphenoid, and closed at its anterior extremity by the frontal bone.

Structures Passing Through the Superior Orbital Fissure:

  • Structures within the tendinous ring:
    • Superior and inferior divisions of the oculomotor nerve, Naso ciliary nerve, abducent nerve, and sympathetic root of the ciliary ganglion.(Option D)
  • Structures above the ring:
    • Trochlear nerve, frontal nerve, lacrimal nerve, lacrimal artery, and superior ophthalmic vein. (Option A)
  • Structures below and medial to the ring:
    • Inferior ophthalmic vein. (Option C)

Key Takeaway:

Ophthalmic Artery does not pass through the superior orbital fissure; it travels through the optic canal.

Superior Orbital Fissure contents MNEMONIC: LOFTS SONIA

  • L: Lacrimal nerve(branch of V1 - Ophthalmic division of Trigeminal nerve)
  • O: Oculomotor nerve(CN III)
  • F: Frontal nerve(branch of V1 - Ophthalmic division of Trigeminal nerve)
  • T: Trochlear nerve(CN IV)
  • S: Superior Ophthalmic vein
  • S: Sympathetic fibres
  • O: Ophthalmic nerve(V1 - Trigeminal nerve, passes as a whole before splitting into branches like Lacrimal, Frontal, and Nasociliary nerves)
  • N: Nasociliary nerve(branch of V1 - Ophthalmic division of Trigeminal nerve)
  • I: Inferior branch of the Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
  • A: Abducens nerve(CN VI)

Other foramens in the Middle Cranial Fossa:

  • Foramen Spinosum: Middle meningeal artery and nerves spinosus.
  • Foramen Ovale: (MALE)
    • Mandibular nerve
    • Accessory middle meningeal artery
    • Lesser petrosal nerve
    • Emissary vein: connecting the pterygoid venous plexus to the cavernous sinus
  • Foramen Rotundum: Maxillary nerve and emissary vein.

Structure passing through the foramen ovale: (M A L E)

question_text: A 32-year-old patient presents with a swelling below the ear and complains of pain in the lobule of the ear. The patient also reports difficulty in completely closing the left eye and experiences trouble while eating food. What nerve is most likely to be damaged in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The facial nerve (CN VII) is the motor nerve of facial expression.
  • It supplies muscles that close the eye, move the mouth, and control movements important for eating and speech.
  • A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen or in the parotid region (swelling below the ear) can cause:
    • Inability to close the eye (orbicularis oculi paralysis)
    • Drooping of the mouth angle → trouble with eating/dribbling
    • Loss of normal facial expressions
    • Pain in the lobule may occur due to the swelling affecting nearby structures, but the motor deficit points directly to facial nerve damage.



Explanation of other options:

Greater Auricular nerve (Option A): Provides cutaneous sensation to the lobule and lower auricle. Damage → sensory loss only, no motor weakness, so cannot explain inability to close eye or eat properly.

Auriculotemporal nerve (Option B): Branch of mandibular nerve (CN V3); supplies sensation to the auricle, external acoustic meatus, and temple. Purely sensory, not motor → would not cause facial muscle weakness.

Vagus nerve (Option D): Auricular branch supplies sensation to concha/external canal. Damage may cause swallowing or phonation issues, but not facial paralysis.

question_text: Which of the following nerve carries the Information travels from the receptors in the organ of Corti of the inner ear (cochlear hair cells) to the central nervous system?
explanation:
The auditory pathway conveys the special sense of hearing.

Information travels from the receptors in the organ of Corti of the inner ear (cochlear hair cells) to the central nervous system, carried by the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII).

This pathway ultimately reaches the primary auditory cortex for conscious perception. In addition, unconscious processing of auditory information occurs in parallel.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy, Volume 2, 3rd Edition, Page number - 878

question_text: A patient presents with periorbital edema, eyelid erythema, chemosis, ptosis and high grade fever with spikes. Patient has history of tonsillitis and otitis media. Examination shows paralysis of extra ocular muscles, loss of pupillary reflex and loss of corneal reflex. Visual acuity is preserved. What is most likely involved with this disease ?
explanation:
The marked arrow in CT scan shows Cavernous sinus.

The given scenario explains paralysis of extra ocular muscles, loss of pupillary reflex and loss of corneal reflex. It means there is paralysis of the oculomotor nerve, trochlear nerve, abducens nerve and ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve. Though optic nerve is spared. This suggest infection of cavernous sinus which is marked above.

High fever with spikes explains Picket fence fever.

Cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) is a rare, life-threatening disorder that can complicate facial infection, sinusitis, orbital cellulitis, pharyngitis, or otitis or following traumatic injury or surgery, especially in the setting of a thrombophilic disorder. Early recognition of cavernous sinus thrombosis which, often presents with fever, headache, eye findings such as periorbital swelling, and ophthalmoplegia, is critical for a good outcome. Despite modern treatment with antibiotics and anticoagulation, the risk of long-term sequelae, such as decreased vision, diplopia, and stroke, remains significant.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and neck, Page number - 430, 437, 536, 668

question_text: Pain from dural irritation in the indicated area is typically referred to which location?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The structure indicated in the image is the posterior cranial fossa. Inflammation of its dura mater can cause referred painradiating to the back of the head and neck.(Option A, C and D ruled out)
  • The cranial dura materreceives its primary innervation from branches of all three divisions of the trigeminal nerve namely:
    • Ophthalmic division (V1)- Tentorial branch
    • Maxillary division (V2)- Nervus meningeus medius
    • Mandibular division (V3)- nervus spinosus
  • The posterior cranial fossa is supplied by C2-C3 fibers via the hypoglossal and vagus nerves to the dura and vessels. Since the overlying skin of the back of the head and neck is innervated by the greater (C2) and third occipital (C3) nerves, dural inflammation produces referred pain in these regions.

Explanation of other options:

Ear (Option A): The external ear receives sensory fibers from the auriculotemporal nerve (V3), auricular branch of vagus (Arnold's nerve), and glossopharyngeal nerve.Thus, ear pain is not typically due to posterior fossa dural irritation.

Vertex (Option C): Pain over the vertex region could be stress headache or occipital neuralgia and referred pain here could arises from supratentorial dura supplied by the ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve (V1)

Mouth (Option D): Pain in the mouth and pharynx is associated with glossopharyngeal (CN IX) and trigeminal (CN V2/V3) innervation, not dura of the posterior fossa.

question_text: Which structure is located in the marked area in the image given below?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The pterygopalatine ganglion is located in the pterygopalatine fossa, behind the maxilla and close to the sphenoid bone.
  • It is associated with the maxillary nerve (V2) and receives parasympathetic fibers via the greater petrosal nerve (from facial nerve, CN VII).
  • These fibers synapse in the ganglion and provide secretomotor innervation to the lacrimal gland, nasal glands, and palatine glands.
  • Hence, a lesion here causes dry eyes and reduced nasal/palatal secretions.

Explanation of Other Options:

Otic ganglion (Option A): Located near foramen ovale, associated with the mandibular nerve (V3); supplies the parotid gland via fibers from glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

Ciliary ganglion (Option B): Found in the orbit, associated with the oculomotor nerve (CN III); controls pupil constriction (sphincter pupillae) and lens accommodation (ciliary muscle).

Submandibular ganglion (Option D): Located near the submandibular gland, associated with the facial nerve (chorda tympani, CN VII); provides secretomotor supply to submandibular and sublingual glands.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Four paired parasympathetic ganglia in the head & neck:
    • Ciliary → CN III → Eye (pupil constriction, accommodation)
    • Pterygopalatine → CN VII → Lacrimal, nasal, palatal glands
    • Submandibular → CN VII → Submandibular & Sublingual glands
    • Otic → CN IX → Parotid gland
  • High-Yield Clinical Correlations:
    • Lesion in pterygopalatine ganglion → Dry eye + decreased nasal secretions.
    • Lesion in otic ganglion → Dry mouth due to loss of parotid secretomotor supply.
    • Lesion in ciliary ganglion → Dilated pupil & loss of accommodation.
    • Lesion in submandibular ganglion → Reduced saliva (submandibular & sublingual).
  • Pterygopalatine ganglia is present at the location marked in the given image.
  • The pterygopalatine ganglion is located in the pterygopalatine fossa, which is found behind the maxilla and near the sphenoid bone.

question_text: A patient presented with weakness of the right side of the face with the loss of pain and temperature.Pain and temperature sensation of the left leg is also lost. The lesion is most likely located at?
explanation:
The above clinical scenario is suggestive of lateral pontine syndrome which occurs due to a lesion located at lateral pons.

Lateral pontine syndrome occurs due to the involvement of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery.

  • Ipsilateral manifestations include:
  • CN VII: Facial paralysis
  • CN V: loss of pain and temperature sensation over the face.
  • Vestibular nerve or nucleus: Horizontal and vertical nystagmus, vertigo, nausea, vomiting, oscillopsia.
  • Auditory nerve or cochlear nucleus: Deafness, tinnitus.
  • Middle cerebellar peduncle: Ataxia of limb and gait.
  • Contralateral manifestations include:
  • Spinothalamic tract: Loss of pain and temperature sensation over the body.

question_text: An 83-year-old man suffers a stroke to the left facial motor nucleus of the pons, resulting in the paralysis of facial nerve. Which of the following motor deficits does he likely experience?
option_a: Mandible deviates to the left when the mouth is opened
option_b: Right corner of the mouth droops when smiling
option_c: Left corner of the mouth droops when smiling
option_d: Unable to wrinkle the forehead on the right side
explanation:
The corners of the mouth are raised by the zygomaticus major muscle, which is innervated by the facial nerve. A lesion in the left facial motor nucleus would cause paralysis of the facial muscles on the same side as the injury, as is the case in this patient.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and neck, page number - 978

question_text: A patient presented with conjugate nystagmus suggestive of a left-sided oculomotor paralysis and diplopia. She also had right-sided hemiplegia.Which of the following is not true regarding this clinical presentation?
option_a: The tectum lies posterior to the cerebral aqueduct
option_b: The superior colliculi are centers for visual reflexes.
option_c: The trochlear nerve emerges in the midline below the superior colliculi.
option_d: The inferior colliculi are auditory centres, and the inferior brachium connects the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate body.
explanation:
The given clinical scenario of contralateral hemiplegia and paralysis of the third cranial nerve is suggestive of Weber syndrome involving the midbrain. In this, the tectum lies posterior to the cerebral aqueduct.

The midbrain connects the pons and cerebellum with the forebrain. Externally, on the posterior surface, there are two pairs of colliculi -the corpora quadrigemina:

  • The superior colliculi are centers for visual reflexes. The superior brachium connects the superior colliculi to the lateral geniculate body and the optic tract.
  • The inferior colliculi are auditory centres, and the inferior brachium connects the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate body.

The trochlear nerve emerges in the midline below the inferior colliculi.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and Neck, Page number - 879

question_text: Which is a source of axons found in the dorsal primary ramus of the 4th thoracic spinal nerve?
option_a: Afferent neurons arising from the skin overlying the trapezius muscle
option_b: Somatic motor neurons supplying the levator scapulae muscle
option_c: Somatic motor neurons supplying the rhomboid muscles
option_d: Somatic motor neurons supplying the trapezius muscle
explanation:
Dorsal primary rami innervate the true back muscles (like erector spinae) and the skin overlying the back. So, they would contain afferent neurons arising from the skin overlying the trapezius muscle. The rhomboid muscles and levator scapulae are not true back muscles. This means that they are innervated by the ventral primary rami of spinal nerves, not the dorsal primary rami. The trapezius receives motor innervation from the accessory nerve--CN XI; it does not receive motor fibers from any spinal nerve.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Back Page number - 901

question_text: A concerned parent brings their 3-month-old baby with an asymmetrical face during crying as shown in the image. Which structure is most likely involved in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient is unable to close his eyes during crying and has smooth nasolabial folds on the left side, pointing towards left infranuclear facial nerve palsy. A lesion at or distal to nucleus of facial nerve causes ipsilateral weakness of entire half of face (both upper and lower parts.)

Explanation of Other Options:

Orbicularis Oculi (Option B)

While it's affected in Bell's Palsy, it doesn't explain the overall facial asymmetry or the underlying neurological issue.

Erb's Palsy (Option C)

Erb's Palsy affects the brachial plexus leading to weakness and paralysis primarily in the shoulder and arm. This patient has no such symptoms.

Cranial nerve 3 (Option D)

Occulomotor nerve primarily controls eye movements (most extraocular muscles), eyelid elevation (levator palpebrae superioris), and pupillary constriction. A lesion here would cause an eye turned "down and out," often with ptosis and dilated pupil.

Key Takeaways:

Infranuclear facial nerve palsy presents as ipsilateral weakness affecting both upper and lower part of face, due to a lesion at or distal to the facial nerve nucleus.

question_text: Risorius is a muscle of ?
explanation: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Facial expression [Ref BDC Vol. III, 5th /e p. 57] The risorius (also risorius muscle, latin: musculus risorius) is a muscle of facial expression located laterally to the mouth opening, which pulls the angle of the mouth laterally. * Origin  - The risorius originates from the masseteric fascia. * Insertion  - The risorius inserts into the skin of the angle of the mouth. * Action  - Upon activation the risorius pulls the angle of the mouth laterally.  - Contractions of the risorius muscle produce facial expression of pleasure and laughter. * Innervation  - The risorius is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII). * Blood supply  - The risorius is mainly supplied by the superior labial branch of the facial artery.

question_text: A 60-year-old male with a history of facial nerve palsy reports difficulty while eating, with food getting trapped between his cheek and teeth. Which muscle is likely affected?

question_text: Which of the following is not a branch of the mandibular nerve?

question_text: Circumvallate papillae of tongue derived from?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The circumvallate papillae (also called vallate papillae) are large, dome-shaped papillae located in front of the sulcus terminalis on the posterior part of the tongue.
  • They are derived from the hypobranchial eminence, which develops from the 3rd pharyngeal arch.
  • Although they are in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (normally 1st arch territory), their nerve supply comes from the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX).

Development of the Tongue

Formation of Anterior Two-Thirds (Option A&B):

  • The lateral lingual swellings overgrow the tuberculum impar and merge to form the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. The line of fusion creates the median sulcus.
  • The tuberculum impar does not contribute to the adult tongue.

Formation of Posterior One-Third:

  • The posterior one-third, including the circumvallate papillae, develops from the cranial part of the hypobranchial eminence.
  • A V-shaped groove (the sulcus terminalis) indicates the fusion line between the anterior and posterior parts.
  • The posterior most part of the tongue and the epiglottis arise from the caudal part of the hypobranchial eminence.

Key takeaways:

The tongue develops from lateral swellings merging to form the anterior two-thirds, with the posterior part arising from the hypobranchial eminence, marked by the sulcus terminalis, and innervated by different cranial nerves based on pharyngeal arch origins.

question_text: The hypobranchial eminence contributes to formation of:

question_text: A patient underwent a left submandibular gland excision during which the hypoglossal nerve was injured. Which of the following deficits would be seen in this case?
option_a: Deviated tongue to the contralateral side
option_b: Deviated tongue to the same side
option_d: Loss of taste in posterior 1/3rd of the tongue
explanation:
Explanation:

The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) provides motor innervation to all intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles (except the palatoglossus).

An injury to the left hypoglossal nerve paralyzes the left genioglossus muscle. This muscle normally protrudes the tongue and deviates it toward the opposite side. When paralyzed, the unopposed action of the right genioglossus muscle causes the tongue to deviate toward the side of the lesion (left) upon protrusion. (Option A ruled out)

Explanation of other options:

Inability to protrude tongue (Option C): Protrusion is still possible due to the functioning contralateral genioglossus muscle, though it will be weak and asymmetrical.

Loss of taste in posterior 1/3rd of the tongue (Option D): Taste sensation for the posterior third of the tongue is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the hypoglossal nerve.

Key Takeaways:

  • A hypoglossal nerve injury causes ipsilateral tongue weakness.
  • Upon protrusion, the tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion.

question_text: During a motorcycle accident, an 18-year-old male landed on the right lateral side of his rib cage with his right upper limb abducted. In the hospital he was found to have "winging" of the right scapula. Which nerve was likely damaged in the accident?
explanation:
An injury to the long thoracic nerve denervates serratus anterior, meaning that there will be no muscle protracting the scapula and counteracting trapezius and the rhomboids, powerful retractors of the scapula. This means that the scapula will be winged backwards, which is this patient's main symptom. The long thoracic nerve is derived from the nerve roots of C5-7. This nerve is particularly vulnerable to iatrogenic injury during surgical procedures, such as mastectomies, because it is located on the superficial side of serratus anterior.

The accessory nerve innervates trapezius an injury to this nerve might lead to an inability to raise the acromion of the shoulder. The lateral pectoral nerve is a small nerve that provides innervation to pectoralis major. The phrenic nerve innervates the diaphragm. The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the thorax and much of the abdominal viscera. The patient's symptoms do not fit with an injury to any of these nerves.

question_text: A patient develops a deformity as shown following overhead weight-lifting exercises. Which muscle is most likely involved?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows a prominent protrusion of the medial border of the scapula, known as winging of the scapula. This finding is most likely due to paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle, resulting from injury to the long thoracic nerve.

Serratus Anterior Muscle

  • The Serratus Anterior muscle is located on the lateral aspect of the thorax.
  • Origin:Upper 8 ribs (anterolateral surface).
  • Insertion:Costal (anterior) surface of scapula.
  • Nerve Supply:Long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7).

Functions

  • Protraction of scapula (pulls scapula forward).
  • Stabilizes scapula against thoracic wall (prevents winging).
  • Lateral rotation of the scapula: Allows glenoid cavity to turn upward, enabling full overhead abduction of the arm.

Clinical Importance

  • Injury to thelong thoracic nerve leads to paralysis of the serratus anterior.
  • Patients will present with:
    • Winging of scapula: The medial border of the scapula protrudes from the thoracic wall.
    • Inability to fully abduct arm overhead.
  • Causes:Post-mastectomy, trauma, weight-lifting injuries.

Explanation of other options:

Trapezius (Option A): Paralysis of the trapezius muscle, due to spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) injury, leads to shoulder drooping and impaired shrugging, but does not produce the classic winging of scapula.

Latissimus dorsi (Option C): The latissimus dorsi muscle, supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve, is responsible for n adduction, extension, and medial rotation of the humerus.

Supraspinatus (Option D): The supraspinatus muscle, innervated by the suprascapular nerve, initiates the first 15° of arm abduction. It does not contribute to scapular stability and is therefore not involved in scapular winging.

question_text: Injury to the pterygopalatine ganglion leads to loss of secretomotor supply to which of the following structures?

question_text: During a physical examination, a physician lightly massages the carotid sinus to evaluate baroreceptor reflex activity in a patient with suspected autonomic dysfunction. The carotid sinus functions as an important sensor in regulating cardiovascular physiology. Which of the following statements regarding the carotid sinus is FALSE?
option_a: It has rich innervation from glossopharyngeal, vagus and sympathetic nerves
option_b: It regulates the blood pressure in the cerebral arteries
option_d: Hypersensitivity on carotid sinuses causes slowing of heart rate
explanation:
Explanation:

The carotid sinus is a baroreceptor, not a chemoreceptor. Chemoreception in the carotid region is primarily handled by the carotid body. (Option C)

Carotid sinus

  • Located at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery
  • Contains stretch receptors that detect changes in arterial blood pressure, thereby helps regulate systemic arterial pressure which influences cerebral perfusion
  • Innervated mainly by the glossopharyngeal nerve (Hering nerve branch, CN IX) and has some vagal sympathetic contributions (Option A)
  • Activation leads to reflex bradycardia and vasodilation to reduce blood pressure (Option D)

Carotid body

  • A nearby but distinct structure which acts as a chemoreceptor detecting oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH levels

Clinical relevance:

  • Carotid sinus hypersensitivity can cause syncope due to exaggerated vagal response leading to bradycardia and hypotension

Key Takeaway:

The carotid sinus is primarily a baroreceptor crucial for blood pressure regulation in the cerebral arteries, while the carotid body serves as a chemoreceptor, monitoring blood gas levels. Understanding these distinctions is essential for grasping cardiovascular physiology and clinical implications.

question_text: Which one of the following is related to the release of bicarbonate in exchange for chloride in the RBC?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Chloride Shift (Hamburger phenomenon) is the exchange of bicarbonate (HCO3-) and chloride (Cl-) ions between RBCs and plasma to maintain electrical neutrality.

CO2+H2O⇌H2CO3⇌H++HCO3-

  • CO2 enters RBCs and reacts with water (H2O) via carbonic anhydrase to form H2CO3 (carbonic acid), which then dissociates into HCO3- (bicarbonate) and H+ (proton).
  • 3- exits the RBC into the plasma, and to maintain electrical neutrality, Cl- enters the RBC (this is the chloride shift).

Explanation of Other Options:

Bohr's effect (Option A)

The Bohr effect describes how increased CO2 and decreased pH lead to a rightward shift in the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, meaning haemoglobin releases more oxygen to tissues. It is related to oxygen unloading in tissues but not directly related to bicarbonate exchange in RBCs.

Haldane effect (Option B)

The Haldane effect describes how deoxygenated hemoglobin binds more CO2 and H+ ions, enhancing CO2 transport in venous blood.

This effect facilitates CO2 loading in tissues and CO2 unloading in the lungs.

None of the above (Option C)

Since Chloride Shift (option C) is correct, this option is incorrect.

Key Takeaways:

The chloride shift involves the exchange of bicarbonate (3-) and chloride (Cl-) ions between RBCs and plasma, helping to maintain electrical neutrality. The Bohr effect relates to oxygen unloading, not bicarbonate exchange. The Haldane effect involves CO2 and H+ ion binding to deoxygenated haemoglobin, aiding CO2 transport. The chloride shift is essential in the transport of CO2 in the blood and is a key physiological process.

question_text: Patient came with symptoms of headache, cognitive and gait impairment, and urinary incontinence. On computed tomography, shows enlargement of the 3rd and both lateral ventricles with a nearly normal size 4th ventricle. Diagnosis of Triventricular hydrocephalus has been made and described as noncommunicating because of;
explanation:
Explanation:

Aqueductal stenosis (AS) is the correct diagnosis. It is a pathological condition causing triventricular obstructive hydrocephalus which requires a clinical and radiological diagnosis.

  • Clinical Features: Patients develop symptoms like headache, cognitive and gait impairment, and urinary incontinence.
  • Imaging Findings: With computed tomography, triventricular hydrocephalus shows enlargement of the 3rd and both lateral ventricles with a nearly normal size 4th ventricle. The cerebral aqueduct (Aqueduct of Sylvius) connects the 3rd and 4th ventricles; therefore, a blockage here causes fluid to back up in the 3rd and lateral ventricles while the 4th ventricle remains normal. This is described as non-communicating hydrocephalus.
  • Management: Treatment options for hydrocephalus due to aqueductal stenosis include insertion of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VP) and Endoscopic Third Ventriculostomy (ETV).

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Cerebrospinal fluid stenosis (Option B): This is not a valid medical term. Stenosis refers to the narrowing of a hollow structure (like a duct or vessel), not the fluid (CSF) itself.
  • Supraoptic stenosis (Option C): This is not a recognized cause of hydrocephalus. The supraoptic region refers to nuclei in the hypothalamus above the optic chiasm, but there is no CSF passage here subject to "stenosis" that would cause this ventricular pattern.
  • Diencephalon stenosis (Option D): This is incorrect terminology. The diencephalon is a solid brain region (thalamus/hypothalamus), not a duct. While a mass in the diencephalon could compress the aqueduct, the condition is defined by the narrowing of the aqueduct itself, not the brain tissue.

question_text: A neurological examination of a 51-year-old woman indicated that she had a loss of pain and temperature sense on the right side of her body, a decreased sense of taste on the left side and hoarseness of voice when speaking. She also complained of dizziness and nausea. Which of the following arteries may be occluded in this patient?
explanation:
The clinical presentation, loss of pain and temperature sensation on the right side of the body, decreased taste sensation on the left side, hoarseness, dizziness, and nausea, suggests a lesion in the lateral medulla, consistent with Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome).

This region is primarily supplied by the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA). Occlusion of PICA can lead to:

  • Contralateral loss of pain and temperature (due to spinothalamic tract involvement)
  • Ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits (e.g., hoarseness from nucleus ambiguus involvement)
  • Vestibular symptoms (e.g., dizziness, nausea)
  • Loss of taste (from nucleus tractus solitarius involvement)

Thus, PICA occlusion is the most likely cause.

The image below shows the blood supply of the medulla.

Explanation of Other Options:

Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA): Supplies the occipital lobe and inferior temporal lobe. Its occlusion typically causes visual disturbances (e.g., contralateral homonymous hemianopia), not lateral medullary symptoms.

Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (AICA): This artery can cause lateral pontine syndrome, which presents with vertigo and cranial nerve deficits, but differs in its pattern and location. Hearing loss is more characteristic of an AICA infarct.

Anterior Spinal Artery: Supplies the medial medulla. Occlusion leads to medial medullary syndrome, characterized by contralateral hemiparesis and loss of proprioception, as well as ipsilateral tongue weakness, which are not the features seen here.

question_text: What fibers is given structure composed of ;
explanation:
Between the cortex, the lateral ventricles, and the deep nuclei lies a mass of fibres connecting distant regions of the brain.

Most of the cerebral fibres have both their origin and termination within the cortex, either in the same hemisphere (association fibres) or opposite hemispheres (commissural fibres) Other fibres connect the cortex to subcortical regions (projection fibres). There are some fibres that, although being located in the cerebral hemispheres do not connect the cortex, but only subcortical structures (e.g. fibres of the anterior commissure connecting the two amygdalae). Fibres group together to form bundles of different diameter and several bundles form larger pathways called fasciculi (or tracts). White matter fasciculi are classified into association, commissural, and projection tracts, although some tracts may contain more than one type of fibre (e.g. the uncinate fasciculus contains both association and projection fibres).

question_text: A patient presented with self-inflicted injuries, auditory hallucinations and delusions. MRI revealed a tumour involving the posterior limb of the internal capsule and the structure medial to it. Which structure is likely to be affected?

The internal capsule separates the thalamus and the caudate nucleus from the lentiform nucleus (globus pallidus + putamen). It is V-shaped in horizontal section and is divided into the anterior limb, genu, posterior limb, retrolenticular part, and sublenticular part. Explanation:

The internal capsule is a white matter tract separating the caudate nucleus from the putamen and globus pallidus, whereas the structure labeled as 4 in the image corresponds to the thalamus, which is a relay center for sensory and motor signals.

Basal Ganglia

  • Basal ganglia are collections of neuron bodies (gray matter) located under the cerebrum, at the base of the brain.
  • Biologically and structurally, they are part of the telencephalon and diencephalon in embryonic development.

Structural Components (belonging to the telencephalon):

  • Caudate Nucleus
    • A C-shaped nucleus with a head, body, and tail. In a transverse section, the head of the caudate nucleus is visible. (Option A)
  • Putamen
    • Along with the globus pallidus, it forms a lens-shaped nucleus called the lentiform nucleus.
    • The putamen is on the lateral side of the lentiform nucleus. (Option C)
  • Globus Pallidus:
    • Located on the medial side of the lentiform nucleus. It is further divided into an external and internal segment. (Option B)
  • Striatum:
    • The caudate nucleus and the putamen together are referred to as the striatum due to grey matter communication between them, creating striations or lines.

Functional Components (not part of the telencephalon):

  • Subthalamic Nucleus:
    • Located under the thalamus and is part of the diencephalon.
  • Substantia Nigra:
    • Located in the midbrain (mesencephalon).
    • It appears dark brown due to neuromelanin, which is involved in the formation of dopamine.
    • Dopamine is a crucial neurotransmitter for the functioning of the basal ganglia.
    • The substantia nigra sends the nigrostriatal pathway to the striatum, which is dopaminergic.
  • Amygdala Nucleus:
    • Part of the limbic system and the Papez circuit, involved in fear and pleasure.
  • Thalamus:
    • Connected to basal ganglia and serves as a relay center.
    • The basal ganglia send information to the ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei of the thalamus, which then project to the motor areas of the cerebral cortex (areas 4 and 6).

The organisation of cranial nerve nuclei in the brainstem follows a dorsal-to-ventral arrangement of afferents and efferents, with somatic afferent nuclei most dorsal and somatic efferent nuclei most ventral.

  • In the embryological development of the neural tube, particularly in the brainstem, the alar plate (sensory) lies dorsally, and the basal plate (motor) lies ventrally.
  • These give rise to functional columns of cranial nerve nuclei, arranged from dorsal to ventral as follows:
    • Afferent (Sensory) Columns - Dorsally placed:
      • Somatic Afferent (SA) - Somatic sensory (e.g., trigeminal sensory nucleus)
      • Visceral Afferent (VA) - Visceral sensory (e.g., nucleus tractus solitarius)
    • Efferent (Motor) Columns - Ventrally placed:
      • Visceral Efferent (VE) - Autonomic motor (e.g., dorsal motor nucleus of vagus)
      • Somatic Efferent (SE) - Somatic motor (e.g., hypoglossal nucleus)
  • This arrangement is preserved in the floor of the fourth ventricle, particularly in the pons and medulla, and helps localise lesions based on clinical presentation.

question_text: What is the correct sequence of the flow of auditory information?
option_a: Eighth nerve > Cochlear nuclei > Superior Olivary nucleus > Lateral lemniscus > Inferior colliculus > Medial Geniculate body > Auditory cortex
option_b: Eighth nerve > Cochlear nuclei > Superior Olivary nucleus > Lateral lemniscus > Medial geniculate body > Inferior colliculus > Auditory cortex
option_c: Eighth nerve > Cochlear nuclei > Auditory cortex > Superior Olivary nucleus > Lateral lemniscus > Inferior colliculus > Medial Geniculate body
option_d: Eighth nerve > auditory cortex > Cochlear nuclei > Superior Olivary nucleus > Lateral lemniscus > Inferior colliculus > Medial Geniculate body
explanation:
The auditory pathway starts at the cochlear nucleus, then the superior olivary complex, then the inferior colliculus, and finally the medial geniculate nucleus. The information is decoded and integrated by each relay nucleus in the pathway and finally projected to the auditory cortex.

The next part of the ascending process of auditory information in the brainstem is the superior olivary nucleus. The superior olivary nucleus takes the information from the cochlear nucleus and begins the process of interpreting and combing information. This begins the process of sound localization through estimating time difference and intensity between each ear

After the superior olivary nucleus, auditory processing continues on to a nucleus called the inferior colliculus (IC). The inferior colliculus (IC) is a midbrain structure that integrates the vast majority of ascending auditory information and projects via the thalamus to the auditory cortex. The IC is also a point of convergence for corticofugal (information from the cerebral cortex) input and input originating outside the auditory pathway. Pathophysiological changes in the IC can alter all aspects of auditory perception and aid in localization of sound.

The medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus then receives the auditory information from the three brainstem nuclei. The information is integrated and the medial geniculate nucleus projects that information to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe of the cerebral cortex.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy, Volume 2, 3rd Edition, Page number - 1127

question_text: What is the correct order in the auditory pathway?
option_a: Cochlea → Spiral Ganglion → Cochlear Nerve → Superior Olivary Nucleus
option_b: Spiral Ganglion → Cochlea → Cochlear Nerve → Superior Olivary Nucleus
option_c: Spiral Ganglion → Cochlear Nerve → Cochlea → Superior Olivary Nucleus
option_d: Cochlea → Spiral Ganglion → Cochlear Nerve → Inferior Olivary Nucleus
explanation:
Explanation:

The auditory pathway begins at the cochlea, where mechanical sound vibrations are transformed into electrical impulses.

  • These impulses are first carried by the spiral ganglion neurons, whose axons constitute the cochlear nerve.
  • The nerve fibres then reach the cochlear nuclei in the brainstem.
  • From there, the signals are relayed to the superior olivary complex, which is the first site for binaural interaction and sound localisation.

Stepwise Pathway of Hearing:

  • Cochlea - sensory transduction of sound waves.
  • Spiral Ganglion - houses the cell bodies of the primary afferent neurons.
  • Cochlear Nerve - carries impulses to the brainstem.
  • Cochlear Nuclei - first synapse in the central auditory system.
  • Superior Olivary Complex - important for comparing sounds from both ears.
  • Lateral Lemniscus - major ascending tract of the auditory system.
  • Inferior Colliculus (midbrain) - integrates auditory inputs.
  • Medial Geniculate Body (thalamus) - final relay before cortex.
  • Primary Auditory Cortex (temporal lobe, Heschl's gyrus) - perception and interpretation of sound.

question_text: Given diagram is showing the microscopic structure of cerebellum. Identify the cells marked with number 2.
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The cells marked with number 2 in the diagram arePurkinje cells, identifiable by their large, flask-shaped cell bodies located in thePurkinje cell layerof the cerebellar cortex.
  • This layer is unique as it consists of only one layer of neurons, making it distinct from other brain regions.
  • Purkinje cells are crucial for motor control and coordination; they send inhibitory signals to the deep cerebellar nuclei, regulating motor output.
  • Their dendrites, which extend into themolecular layer, form a complex branching structure that integrates signals from numerous synapses, reflecting their role in processing sensory and motor information.
  • The axons of Purkinje cells descend through thegranular layerto reach the white matter, influencing cerebellar output.
  • The neurons of the cerebellar cortex are of five main types:
    • Purkinje cells: forming the layer named after them
    • Granule cells: forming the granular layer, these small neurons lack the distinct morphology of Purkinje cells and do not form a single layer.
    • Outer (external) stellate cells: lying in molecular layer
    • Basket cells: Has a pyramidal or oval shape, measures about 15 μm in length, and lies in the lower third of the molecular layer just above the Purkinje cells
    • Golgi cells: Present in the granular layer. Golgi cells are irregularly rounded or polygonal GABAergic, inhibitory interneurones: they number approximately 1 per 1.5 Purkinje cells in the human brain.

Why Not Others:

  • B (Granular Cells): Located in the granular layer, C (Basket Cells): These cells, found in the molecular layer, have a different structure and primarily function to modulate the activity of Purkinje cells, rather than forming the identifiable layer.
  • D (Golgi Cells): Present in the granular layer, , but they are not flask-shaped like Purkinje cells.

Key Takeaways:

  • Purkinje cellsare the defining neurons of the cerebellar cortex, forming a single layer of large, flask-shaped cells crucial for motor coordination.
  • Their extensive dendritic trees allow complex processing of motor signals, highlighting their essential role in balance and coordination.

question_text: Which of the following structures does the cell pointed in arrow inhibit?
explanation:
The image shows a histopathological section of the cerebellum. The cells marked with the arrow are Purkinje cells and they inhibit deep nuclei of the cerebellum.

The cerebellar cortex is divided into 3 layers. They are:

  • Molecular layer - It is the outermost layer. It contains stellate cells and basket cells. They receive excitatory input from the parallel fibers and form inhibitory synapses on the Purkinje cells. It contains many myelinated and unmyelinated nerve fibers giving it a pale appearance in H and E staining.

Purkinje layer - It is the middle layer. It contain flask-shaped cell bodies of Purkinje cells. Their dendrites pass into the molecular layer. The axons of the Purkinje cells passes through the granular layer into the white matter and synapses with the cerebellar nuclei.

Granular layer - It is the innermost layer. It contains the cell bodies of the granule cells as well as Golgi cells. It receives excitatory input from the mossy fibers. They end on the dendrites of the granule cells and these complexes are called glomeruli. The axon from the granule cells travels to the molecular layer and bifurcates in a T-shape. These branches form the T and are called parallel fibers. These parallel fibers form excitatory synapses with the Purkinje cells. The granule cells form the only excitatory neurons in the cerebellar cortex.

Golgi cells receive input from parallel fibers and mossy fibers. They send inhibitory output to the granule cells.

Meckel's diverticulum is from the vitelline duct. Urachal fistula is a persistent allantoic duct. Cystic kidney results from failure of the collecting ducts to meet the metanephric blastema. Spina bifida cystica is a herniation of the spinal cord through a defective vertebral arch.

question_text: A neuron with a cell body in the dorsal root ganglia could convey what type of fibers?
option_a: Motor to the deep back muscles
option_b: Motor to the pectoralis major muscle
option_c: Sensory from the skin overlying the trapezius
option_d: Sympathetic preganglionics to the suprarenal medulla
explanation:
The dorsal root ganglia is the location of the cell bodies of somatic sensory neurons. Cells from the dorsal root ganglia transmit somatic sensation from areas like the skin to the central nervous system. A neuron with a cell body in the dorsal root ganglia might be involved in conveying sensory information from the skin overlying the trapezius.

Motor neurons have their cell bodies in the ventral horn of the spinal cord. They leave the spinal nerve through the ventral root, join a spinal nerve, and then divide into the ventral and dorsal primary rami. The dorsal primary rami innervate the deep back muscles, while the ventral primary rami innervate other muscles, including pectoralis major (which is innervated via the brachial plexus).

The cell bodies of preganglionic sympathetic fibers are found in the lateral horn of the spinal cord. Finally, visceral afferent sensation is not carried on somatic sensory neurons--instead, the sensation from the stomach is carried on special visceral afferent nerves which accompany sympathetic nerves.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Back Page number - 893

question_text: What is not true about the marked structure?
option_a: A gate control exists by which peripheral afferents and descending pathways can modulate sensory transmission.
option_b: Involved in the transmission and modulation of pain, temperature, and touch.
option_c: Many cells are local interneurons and likely play an important role as inhibitory and excitatory interneurons that regulate local excitability
option_d: The substantia gelatinosa of Rolando(SGR) is a white matter structure of the dorsal spinal cord
explanation:
The substantia gelatinosa of Rolando

(SGR) is a grey matter structure of the dorsal spinal cord primarily involved in the transmission and modulation of pain, temperature, and touch.

A gate control exists by which peripheral afferents and descending pathways can modulate sensory transmission. Evidence is presented that the mechanism may exist in the substantia gelatinosa laminae Il and Ill.

The substantia gelatinosa contains numerous cell types.

Many cells are local interneurons and likely play an important role as inhibitory and excitatory interneurons that regulate local excitability; however, some of these cells clearly project rostrally.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and neck, Page number - 841

question_text: Loss of sense of vibration and position in case of Dejerine syndrome is due to damage to which of the following structure?
explanation:
Explanation:

Dejerine (median medullary) syndrome occurs due to anterior spinal artery occlusion and classically involves three structures: The pyramid causing contralateral hemiplegia, medial lemniscus causing loss of vibration and position sense, and the hypoglossal nerve causing ipsilateral tongue paralysis. The olivary complex and arcuate nucleus are not a part of medial medullary region involved in this syndrome, hence do not produce dorsal column sensory loss.

question_text: The marked ligament is modification of ?
option_a: Bilateral triangular lateral extensions of pia mater
option_b: Bilateral triangular lateral extensions of dura mater
option_c: Bilateral quadrangle lateral extensions of pia mater
option_d: Unilateral lateral extensions of pia mater
explanation:
The denticulate ligaments are bilateral triangular lateral extensions of pia mater that anchor the spinal cord to the dura mater.

They are formed by pia mater of the spinal cord coursing in-between the dorsal and ventral nerve roots bilaterally. They function to provide stability to the spinal cord within the vertebral canal 1-3. There are usually 21 pairs evenly spaced along the length of the spinal cord but their number can range from 18 to 24 pairs. The first (superiormost) pair inserts into the lateral borders of the foramen magnum, with the vertebral artery anterior to them and the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) posterior. The inferiormost pair is at the level of the conus medullaris, namely, between the T12 and L1 segmental nerve roots, and its pia mater fuses with the filum terminale.

Reference: Textbook of Gray';s Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and neck Page number - 104

question_text: Which of the following is most preferred site for lumbar puncture?
option_a: Disc between L1 and L2 vertebra
option_b: Disc between L2 and L3 vertebra
option_c: Disc between L3 and L4 vertebra
option_d: Disc between L4 and L5 vertebra
explanation:
Explanation:

LP is performed below the termination of spinal cord, and the most preferred site is the disc between L3 and L4 vertebra. This space is safely located below conus medullaris and provides a roomy subarachnoid space containing only cauda equina nerve roots.

question_text: Your 27-year old patient displays ataxia when asked to walk across the examination room. You ask him to stand still with his eyes closed and note marked swaying back and forth. When he opens his eyes the swaying persists. Vibration sense is normal on all four limbs. Given the clinical picture in this case, such ataxia is likely due to damage to which of the following structures?
option_c: Posterior limb of the internal capsule
explanation:
The patient's ataxia and swaying, which persist even when his eyes are open, suggest a problem with the cerebellum. The cerebellum is responsible for coordinating movement and maintaining balance.

Damage to the cerebellum can result in unsteady and uncoordinated movements, leading to ataxia. The normal vibration sense on all four limbs indicates that the dorsal columns, which transmit sensory information such as vibration sense, are intact. The cerebral peduncles, posterior limb of the internal capsule, and ventral horns of the spinal cord are not directly involved in coordinating movement and balance, making them less likely to be the cause of the patient's symptoms.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and Neck, Page number - 841

question_text: Which of the following is correct for the Fasciculus Gracilis and Fasciculus cuneatus ?
option_a: The gracile and cuneate fasciculi, collectively called the anterior columns.
option_b:
Heavily myelinated primary sensory fibers that convey proprioceptive, tactile, and vibratory
information from the ipsilateral side of the body
option_c: Heavily myelinated primary sensory fibers that convey proprioceptive, tactile, and vibratory information from the contralateral side of the body
option_d: Pain signals may also be transmitted via the anterior columns, especially the gracile fasciculus, from the pelvic viscera to the thalamus.
explanation:
The gracile and cuneate fasciculi, collectively called the posterior columns, are composed of the central processes of heavily myelinated primary sensory fibers that convey proprioceptive, tactile, and vibratory

information from the ipsilateral side of the body. Fibers in the gracile fasciculus originate from sacral, lumbar, and lower thoracic (below T6) levels; those in the cuneate fasciculus originate from upper thoracic (above T6) and cervical levels. Injury to the posterior columns on one side results in a loss of proprioception, discriminative touch, and vibratory sense below the level of the lesion on the same side. However, there is clinical evidence that pain signals may also be transmitted via the posterior columns, especially the gracile fasciculus, from the pelvic viscera to the thalamus. Comparable information may also ascend through the cuneate fasciculus. This information is most likely processed through the postsynaptic posterior column system.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and neck, Page number - 879

question_text: Myelination
option_a: Is accomplished by neurilemma or Schwann cells in peripheral nerves
option_b: Is accomplished by oligodendroglial cells within the spinal cord
option_d: All of the above are correct
explanation:
Schwann cells do the myelination peripherally, while oligodendroglia cells do it centrally. Myelination continues for a year postnatally. The myelin coating is extremely important to nerve conduction velocity along the nerve.

question_text: At 24 weeks of intrauterine life the spinal cord presents up to which of the following vertebral level?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Positional changes of the spinal cord occur due to differential growth between the spinal cord and vertebral column:

Termination of spinal cord in relation to vertebral canal at various stages of development:

Termination of spinal cord in relation to vertebral canal at various stages of development:

  • Up to the 3rd month of intrauterine development, the spinal cord extends throughout the entire length of the vertebral canal (Option A).
  • At week 18, the lower end of spinal cord ends at S3 vertebrae (Option B).
  • At week 24, the lower end of spinal cord ends at S1 vertebrae.
  • At birth, the lower end of spinal cord ends at the level of L3 vertebrae (Option D).

Key takeaway:

At 24 weeks, the spinal cord terminates at S1, and positional changes are crucial for avoiding spinal cord injury during procedures like lumbar punctures.

explanation:
After entering the spinal cord the first order neurons synapse (in the nucleus proprius), and the second order neurons decussate via the anterior white commissure. These second order neurons ascend synapsing in the VPL of the thalamus. Incoming first order neurons can ascend or descend via the Lissauer tract.

question_text: The myelogram also revealed that the dorsal and ventral rootlets of the 5th and 6th cervical nerves had been avulsed (torn or pulled out) from the spinal cord on the right side. Which nerve fibers would not be damaged by the avulsion?
explanation:
Somatic afferent neurons originate from the dorsal root and dorsal rootlets. If dorsal rootlets were avulsed, somatic afferent nerve fibers would be damaged. Somatic efferent neurons originate from the ventral root and ventral rootlets. If ventral rootlets were avulsed, somatic efferent nerve fibers would be damaged. Preganglionic (presynaptic) sympathetic neurons originate from the lateral horn of the spinal cord between the levels of T1 and L2. They exit the spinal cord through the ventral rootlets and eventually synapse at sympathetic ganglia. Since they travel through the ventral rootlets, the preganglionic sympathetic neurons would be damaged by the avulsion of ventral rootlets between T1 and L2, but not in cervical regions. The postganglionic sympathetic fibers would not be disrupted by avulsing the dorsal and ventral rootlets in any region. They orginate in the sympathetic ganglia which are not a part of the spinal cord. (There will be much more to come on ganglia later on--stay tuned!)

Reference- Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Back Page number - 901

question_text: Which structure does NOT contain efferent autonomic nerve fibers?
explanation:
The dorsal root of a spinal nerve contains afferent sensory nerve fibers and no efferent autonomic nerve fibers. The efferent autonomic nerve fibers, which originate in the lateral horn of the spinal nerve, travel out of the spinal cord through the ventral root of the spinal nerve. As the ventral and dorsal roots join to form the spinal nerve, the fibers from both roots intermingle, and the dorsal and ventral primary rami take a mix of fibers, including afferent sensory fibers from the dorsal root, and efferent motor fibers from the ventral root. Postganglionic sympathetic efferent fibers join each spinal nerve via a gray ramus communicans. So, all of the other nerves listed do contain efferent autonomic fibers.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and neck, Page number - 841

explanation:
Pathway of fine touch:

  • The central processes of the neurons in the dorsal nerve root ganglia enter the posterior white column of the spinal cord and form the fasciculus gracilis and the fasciculus cuneatus.
  • These are uncrossed tracts.
  • The second neuron lies in the nucleus gracilis or nucleus cuneatus. It gives off the internal arcuate fibres which cross to the opposite side through the sensory decussation.

explanation:

question_text: It is decided to image the spinal cord and spinal nerve rootlets by doing a myelogram (injection of a radio-opaque dye into the subarachnoid space followed by a radiograph). In order to inject the dye without injury to the spinal cord, the injection is usually done below what vertebral level?
explanation:
In an adult, the spinal cord usually ends at the inferior border of L1 or the superior border of L2. Therefore, it is relatively safe to insert a needle above or below L4. At this level, the nerve roots are suspended in the CSF and can float away from the pressure of the needle, so these roots will not be damaged by the needle.

How can you find the L4 level on a patient? If you find the tops of the 2 iliac crests and draw a line connecting them, that line should be going through the spinous processes of the L4 vertebra.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Back, Page number - 104

question_text: The myelogram revealed that the dye had leaked out along the spinal nerves in the mid cervical region on the right side. For the dye to leak out, what layer must have been torn or ruptured?
explanation:
The previous question stated that a myelogram is a radiograph taken following injection of a radio-opaque dye into the subarachnoid space. So, it should make sense that the arachnoid must be ruptured for the dye to leak out following this procedure. Denticulate ligaments are specializations of the pia mater that form a longitudinal shelf separating the dorsal and ventral rootlets. They suspend the spinal cord in the subarachnoid space. These ligaments would not be disturbed during a myelogram. Periostium is a fibrous connective tissue that invests bones, and perineurium is a connective tissue covering that encloses a fasicle of peripheral nerve fibers. The pia mater is the innermost covering of the spinal cord. It closely follows the entire spinal cord and is not penetrated during a myelogram

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Back, Page number - 103

question_text: The conus medullaris:
option_a: Exhibits both a cervical and lumbar enlargement
option_b: Has a modification of neural tissue extending from its termination to the coccygeal ligament
option_c: Gives origin to most of the cauda equina
option_d: Is found at its lowest extent at S2
explanation:
Located at L2, the conus medullarus is the tapered termination of the spinal cord proper. Most of the cauda equina originate from the conus medullaris and then travel to the vertebral foramina inferior. Although the spinal cord exhibits both a cervical and a lumbar enlargement, the conus medullaris refers to the termination of the spinal cord, not the entire spinal cord.

There is no modified neural tissue extending from the termination of the conus medullaris to the coccygeal ligament. Instead, the filum terminal internum, which is a thread-like extension of the pia mater, extends from the conus medullaris. Eventually, this filum terminal internum becomes enclosed in the filum terminale externum, which is a thread-like extension of the dura mater extending below the end of the dural sac (at the S2 level). The filum terminal externum is what attaches to the coccyx, forming the coccygeal ligament.

The conus medullaris is located at L2, at the termination of the spinal cord. The dural sac, however, continues to the S2 level. (These are important levels to keep in mind!) Finally, the conus medularis is not anesthetized to perform a spinal tap--hopefully, the needle used for a spinal tap won't even touch the conus medullaris!

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Back, Page number - 103

question_text: A 45-year-old man complained to his physician that the muscles of his upper limb were weak and he felt clumsy while walking. Tests revealed that he had amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Lou Gehrig's disease), a disease which attacks the neurons of the voluntary motor system. Where would one expect to see atrophic or degenerated nerve cell bodies?
option_a: Dorsal horn of the spinal cord
option_c: Lateral horn of the spinal cord
option_d: Ventral horn of the spinal cord
explanation:
The cell bodies of the motor neurons are found in the ventral horn of the spinal cord. Since these are the cells that are being degraded in ALS, which is destroying the voluntary motor system, this is the place where you would expect to see the atrophied cell bodies.

The dorsal horn of the spinal cord contains the cell bodies that the afferent sensory neurons synapse on before the neural signal ascends the spinal cord. The dorsal root ganglion contains the cell bodies for the somatic sensory neurons. The lateral horn of the spinal cord contains the cell bodies of the presynaptic sympathetic neurons. The sympathetic chain ganglion contains the cell bodies of the postsynaptic sympathetic neurons. Remember--sympathetic neurons can provide motor innervation to structures, but not voluntary motor innervation!

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Back, Page number - 104

option_d: Transverse processes, pedicles and ligamenta flavum

question_text: In an adult, the conus medullaris of the spinal cord is normally positioned at which vertebral body levels:
explanation:
In adults, the conus medullaris is normally positioned between T12 and L2. This is why it is safe to do a lumbar puncture at the level of L4.
