question_text:
30 years old male met with a road traffic accident. He was taken to hospital and under gone with CT scan of spine. He was diagnosed with Brown-Sequard syndrome at the level of T12 Spine. All of the following symptoms are seen below the level of injury, EXCEPT:
(A): Contralateral loss of touch sensation
(B): Contralateral loss of conscious proprioceptive sensations
(C): Contralateral loss of pain sensation
(D): Contralateral loss of temperature sensation
option_b: Contralateral loss of conscious proprioceptive sensations
explanation:
Explanation:

Brown-Sequard syndrome is due to hemisection of spinal cord. Below the lesion, the posterior column (carrying conscious proprioception) remains ipsilateral, so proprioception loss occurs on the same side, not contralaterally. Hnece, option B is incorrect.

The spinothalmic tracts that carry pain, temperature and crude touch, cross to the opposite side 1-2 segments above where it enters the spinal cord. Hence, contralateral loss of touch, pain and temperature occurs.

question_text: Which of the following is true about syringomyelia?
option_a: Bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensations below the lesion
option_b: Bilateral loss of touch and pressure sensations below the lesion
option_c: Bilateral loss of conscious proprioceptive sensations
option_d: Bilateral loss of vibratory and joint position sensation
explanation:
Explanation:

Syringomyelia occurs when a fluid filled cavity develops in the centre of spinal cord, usually in the cervical region, destroying the tissue around central canal. This damages the decussating spinothalmic fibres in anterior white commissure so that there is bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the lesion.

Other sensations like touch, proprioception, vibration are carried by posterior column fibres that do not cross here, so they remain preserved.

question_text: Which of the following lemniscus is a part of auditory pathway
explanation:
Explanation:

On the ventral part of pons bands of fibres made up (from medial to lateral side)

  • Medial lemniscus
  • Spinal lemniscus
  • Trigeminal lemniscus
  • Lateral lemniscus

The lateral lemniscus is the only one that forms a major component of the auditory pathway, carrying fibres from the cochlear nuclei via trapezoid body and superior olivary complex up to the inferior colliculus.

Medial, spinal and trigeminal lemnisci carry touch, pain temperature, and trigeminal sensory fibres respectively, and are not a part of hearing.

question_text: Visceral pain is often referred to a site on the body wall (where the patient "feels" it) that is innervated by the same spinal cord segment that innervates the visceral organ involved. Pain of appendicitis is often first felt around the umbilicus, indicating that the appendix receives its sympathetic (and thus visceral afferents) from which spinal cord segment?
explanation:
Sensation from around the umbilicus is mediated by T10. This is an important landmark to remember!

question_text: A 40-year-old male patient visited the hospital with a complaint of involuntary urination. He has a history of spinal cord injury at the T11 level in an accident a month ago. He is unable to initiate urination voluntarily, and he experiences involuntary urine leakage, especially when the bladder is full. What is the diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

Automatic reflex bladder occurs in patients with spinal cord injuries above the sacral micturition centre (S2 - S4), leading to upper motor neuron lesion.

This condition causes the bladder to empty reflexively when it becomes full, without voluntary control.

Atonic bladder and Cauda equina syndrome occur with lower motor neuron lesions, leading to a flaccid bladder that cannot contract properly and causes urinary retention, rather than involuntary leakage (Options B and C).

Stress incontinence is related to weakened pelvic floor muscles, not a spinal cord injury. It leads to incontinence during increased abdominal pressure, with coughing and sneezing (Option D).

question_text: At what level does the spinal cord end in infants?
explanation:
Explanation:

At birth, the spinal cord extends down to L3, but as the child grows, the vertebral column elongates more than the spinal cord, and by adulthood, it typically ends at L1-L2.

  • The spinal cord occupies the superior two-thirds of the vertebral canal.
  • It is continuous cranially with the medulla oblongata, just below the level of the foramen magnum, at the upper border of the atlas.
  • It terminates caudally as the conus medullaris.
  • During development, the vertebral column elongates more rapidly than the spinal cord, so that there is an increasing discrepancy between the anatomical level of spinal cord segments and their corresponding vertebrae.
  • At Carnegie stage 23 of development, the vertebral column and spinal cord are the same length and the cord ends at the last coccygeal vertebra.
  • In later fetal life, the conus medullaris lies between L3 and S5 vertebrae.
  • In premature and term neonates, it lies between the first and third lumbar vertebrae.
  • In children between the ages of 1 and 7 years, it lies between the T12 and L3 vertebrae.
  • In the adult, the spinal cord terminates on average at the level of the middle third of the body of the L1 vertebra, which corresponds approximately to the transpyloric plane.

Key Takeaways:

Spinal Cord Termination in Different Ages

question_text: A person is able to maintain balance immediately after a rollercoaster ride. Which of the following is the most likely involved in normal balance maintenance?
explanation:
Explanation:

A rollercoaster ride strongly stimulates the vestibular system in the inner ear, which is responsible for sensing head position and movement and is crucial for maintaining balance through vestibulospinal tract.

Vestibulospinal tract:

  • Location: Anterior white column of spinal cord
  • Function: Unconscious maintenance of the posture and balance
  • The fibres arise from the lateral vestibular nucleus lying at the pontomedullary junction.
  • The fibres descend uncrossed to the spinal cord.
  • This tract is situated in the anterior white column of the spinal cord.
  • These fibres synapse with anterior horn cells. It has two types:
    • Lateral Vestibulospinal Tract: Controls trunk and limb extensor (anti-gravity) muscles to maintain upright posture and balance against gravity.
    • Medial Vestibulospinal Tract: Controls head and neck muscles for stabilizing head position and coordinating head/eye movements.

Explanation of Other Options:

Corticospinal tract (Option A)

This tract primarily controls voluntary motor movements, especially fine motor skills, but is not directly involved in automatic balance maintenance.

Corticobulbar tract (Option B)

This tract controls voluntary movements of the face and head via cranial nerves, not balance or posture.

Reticulospinal tract (Option D)

While involved in locomotion and some aspects of posture, the reticulospinal tract is less specific for balance maintenance immediately after vestibular stimulation compared to the vestibulospinal tract.

Key takeaway:

The vestibulospinal tract plays a key role in maintaining balance and posture through unconscious motor control, especially following disturbances such as after a rollercoaster ride.

question_text: Damage to anterior spinothalamic tract leads to Loss of:
option_a: Contralateral loss of light pain and temperature below the level of the lesion
option_b: Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature below the level of the lesion
option_c: Contralateral loss of light touch and pressure below the level of the lesion
option_d: Ipsilateral loss of light touch and pressure below the level of the lesion
explanation:
Explanation:

The anterior spinothalamic tract carries light touch and pressure, and because its fibres decussate (cross) and then ascend upwards to the thalamus, hence a lesion causes CONTRALATERAL loss of these sensations below the level of injury.

Lateral spinothamic tract mediates pain and temperature, the dorsal column mediates fine touch and conscious proprioception, and spinocerebellar tracts mediate unconscious proprioception and coordination.

question_text: A patient presents with muscle wasting, reduced tone, and weakness of the right hand. Fine motor movements, such as dough kneading, are also affected. Which of the following structures is most likely to be impaired in this patient?
option_a: Anterior grey horn of the spinal cord in the cervical region
option_c: Corticospinal tract in the cervical region
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical features and signs presented by the patient strongly suggest lower motor neuron (LMN) involvement, specifically affecting the hand muscles. The anterior (ventral) grey horn of the spinal cord contains the cell bodies of lower motor neurons (LMNs) that innervate skeletal muscles.

In the cervical region, especially segments C8–T1, these LMNs supply the intrinsic muscles of the hand.

Damage here causes:

  • Flaccid paralysis
  • Muscle wasting (atrophy)
  • Fasciculations (sometimes)
  • Loss of fine motor control

Explanation of other options:

Internal capsule (Option B): Would cause upper motor neuron (UMN) signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia) and involve more extensive areas (not isolated hand wasting)

Corticospinal tract in the cervical region(Option C): Causes UMN signs (no wasting), often affects both upper and lower limbs on the same side

Brainstem (Option D): likely affects cranial nerves, not just the hand; more generalised or bilateral signs would be expected in case of brain stem injury.

question_text: A patient presents with Lower back pain, Buttock pain, Leg pain, Chronic tension/tightness; also known as tight hamstrings, Lower leg pain, Tingling and Pins & Needles sensation. The patient later diagnosed with spinal cord degeneration. Entrapment of nerve is shown in the image below. Which nerve is it?
explanation:
Sciatic Nerve Entrapment (SNE) is when the sciatic nerve becomes adhered to surrounding tissues, typically at the deep glute muscles in the back of the hip, causing a loss of the normal slide and glide that is required for healthy nerve function.

The entrapment is caused by chronically-developed fibrotic adhesions that form around the nerve and tether it to the surrounding muscles.

When the nerve is entrapped and unable to move normally, it can produce sciatic-like symptoms.

A challenge for patients is that this condition is unlikely to be reported in diagnostic imaging. It's not uncommon for a patient to present an MRI report which has been tagged as clear of any pathology, and lacking any explanation for their symptoms. Yet, they still experience ongoing lower back, hip and/or leg symptom.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Lower Limb, Page number - 579

question_text: Exteroceptive sensation passes through which of the following tract?
explanation:
Explanation:

The dorsal column tracts (fasciculus gracillis and fasciculus cuneatus) carry exteroceptive sensations such as touch-pressure, along with proprioception and vibratory sensations, via myelinated fibres ascending to the dorsal column nuclei in the medulla.

Spino-cerebellar tracts carry coordination, spino-thalmic tracts carry pain and spino-reticular tracts carry awareness.

question_text: In Angina pectoris, which nerve is involved in radiation of chest pain to the left arm?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In angina pectoris, myocardial anoxia stimulates visceral afferent fibers from the heart.
  • These fibers travel via cervical cardiac nerves and thoracic splanchnic nerves to the sympathetic chain and enter the spinal cord at T1-T4 segments.
  • Because visceral and somatic afferents converge at the same spinal levels, the pain is referred to regions supplied by these dermatomes.
  • The T2 dermatome corresponds to the upper medial arm, axilla, and some part of the upper chest.
  • The intercostobrachial nerve is the lateral cutaneous branch of the second intercostal nerve (T2), carries the referred pain to the medial side of the left arm
  • This, explains the characteristic chest pain radiating to the arm in anghina pectoris.

question_text: Preganglionic parasympathetic nerve fibers within the pelvic (inferior hypogastric) plexus arise from S2, 3, 4 and enter the plexus via:
explanation:
Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry parasympathetic fibers from the lateral horn of the spinal cord at the S2, 3, and 4 levels. They can be seen coming off of the ventral primary rami of S2, 3, and 4 and going to the inferior hypogastric plexus. These nerves provide parasympathetic innervation to the pelvic viscera and the GI tract distal to the left colic flexure. (Remember, the vagus gives parasympathetic innervation to the rest of the gut.) Sacral splanchnic nerves come off the sacral sympathetic chain ganglia, carrying sympathetic fibers that will go to the inferior hypogastric plexus. To remember the difference between the pelvic and sacral splanchnics, just remember that the sacral splanchnics are named after a spinal cord segment, just like the thoracic, lumbar, and cervical splanchnics that you know and love. These all carry sympathetic fibers. Pelvic splanchnics are not named after a spinal cord segment and they're different they carry parasympathetic fibers.

Conus medullaris syndrome results from injury to the S2-S4 spinal cord segments, producing perineal anaesthesia, early bladder and bowel involvement due to sacral parasympathetic loss, and impaired sexual functions. Hence, all the features mentioned are features of conus medullaris syndrome.

question_text: The fibres of tract of Lissauer give axons to which of the following nuclei?
explanation:
Explanation:

The tract of Lissauer lies at the dorsolateral part of the spinal cord and carries fine myelinated and unmyelinated fibres from the dorsal roots, which ascent or descend 1-2 segments before giving collaterals. These fibres mainly end in the substantia gelatinosa. They do not project to deeper dorsal horn nuclei nucleus proprius and Clark's column.

explanation:
The sympathetic fibers in the greater thoracic splanchnic nerve are preganglionic sympathetic fibers that have left the sympathetic chain and are going to synapse in abdominal ganglia. These preganglionic sympathetic fibers originate in the lateral horn of the spinal cord grey matter. The celiac ganglia and the superior mesenteric ganglia are the two ganglia where the fibers from the greater thoracic splanchnic nerve can go to synapse. Finally, remember that these fibers did not originate in the chain ganglia--the fibers from there are the postganglionic sympathetic fibers.

question_text: Which of the following nerve is involved in cremasteric reflex?
explanation:
Explanation:

Genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster muscle so involved in cremasteric reflex.

Cremasteric reflex:

Upon stroking the skin of upper part of medial side of thigh, there is reflex contraction of cremaster muscle, as evidenced by elevation and retraction of the testis. It is brisker in children.

  • Afferent limb (sensory): Ilioinguinal nerve (L1) carries sensation from the skin of the upper medial thigh (Option D).
  • Efferent limb (motor): Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2) - supplies the cremaster muscle, leading to elevation of the testis.
  • Spinal segment involved: L1-L2
  • Femoral nerve (Option A): Supplies anterior thigh muscles (quadriceps) and skin of anterior thigh; not involved in the reflex arc.
  • Iliohypogastric nerve (Option B): Supplies the lower abdominal wall and suprapubic skin; no role in the cremasteric reflex.

Key takeaways:

The cremaster muscle supports and elevates the testis and is involved in the cremasteric reflex, which causes testicular retraction upon thigh stimulation.
